current-cbo-cost-estimates.coverageStatement: Sampled. CBO estimates linked to held bills from the 108th Congress onward, combining BILLSTATUS metadata and per-Congress CBO feeds. The 112th and 113th use the feed alone. A Congress's feed contributes only after a scoped run reads it. Items without a bill link stay in `cbo_feed_items`. Missing rows do not prove CBO never scored a bill; a weekly estimate may cover several bills. CBO document bodies are not acquired.
current-cbo-cost-estimates.qualityNotes: The bill's cbo_cost_estimates_outcome distinguishes an absent or empty element, an unexpected shape, and populated estimates. An empty index does not establish that CBO never scored the bill. Report citations are the bill's list, not proof that each publication is reprinted in each report; the report's recital gate is evaluated separately. A feed row carries its bill's own BILLSTATUS report citations, read by the same run or carried from the bill's published rows, and NULL where neither names them. A successfully evaluated bill replaces its prior BILLSTATUS rows, including when the list is absent or empty; an unexpected list shape retains prior rows until a successful read can establish the current relationships. A feed read replaces its Congress's prior feed rows, so an item CBO withdraws or re-files leaves, and a feed that cannot be read keeps them. `found_by` says how each row names its bill; the rows published before it take `billstatus` in a one-time backfill. `title_bill_id` is the bill the estimate's title leads with: where it differs from `bill_id` (7 of the 12,732 BILLSTATUS rows on 2026-09-29), `bill_id` is a numbering error as published and `title_bill_id` the bill scored. A title leading with a public law reads through the published `laws` table, which held the 119th Congress alone on 2026-09-29, so such a title of an earlier Congress leaves `title_bill_id` NULL and a blank feed item titled by an earlier law has no row (110th P.L. 110-50 and 112th P.L. 112-8). CBO's 119th-Congress feed, read 2026-10-03, holds 53 items that name no bill and have no row, 48 of them weekly suspension estimates. 23 of them are among the feed's 674 items dated 2026: 21 suspension estimates, 62413 (reconciliation recommendations of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs committee) and 62643 (the Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027).

current-comment-periods.coverageStatement: Derived, and bounded by its inputs: every `federal_register` record with a `comments_close_on`, every `documents` row with a comment end date, and every Register record such a document copies lands in exactly one period, anchored or not. Left out are windows that close before they open, placeholder closes (see data quality), and legacy Regulations.gov documents that state a comment end but neither a comment start nor a posting date (all closing by 2011); the builder logs each count. Native row counts remain unknown until an exact admitted input and reader supply them.
current-comment-periods.qualityNotes: For date-range discovery, test all three date columns (`close_date`, `register_close_date` and `regulations_gov_close_date`). They can concern different purposes, including comments, replies, objections, hearings or petitions; the builder does not classify legal submission purpose. `close_date` is the maximum normalized close among grouped records, not the legally controlling/current deadline. The source-specific columns retain each source's maximum; a difference is not resolved by choosing the later value. Base Federal Register dates remain historical statements of each dated publication, not current status, and Regulations.gov records can update independently. Inspect source filing instructions and later notices; neither title matching nor a shared docket/RIN proves legal effect. Extension/correction documents with NULL dates can exist outside these windows, and NULL does not establish no deadline. A close on or after 2050-01-01 is a placeholder and states nothing: the inputs hold no close from 2033 to 2049, and every later one is a stand-in (Regulations.gov's 2099 and 2100 dates, FDA's 2050-02-21 open dockets, Register year typos such as 3008 for 2008). A record whose only close is a placeholder, or whose window closes before it opens, adds no dates; it is listed only as its notice's Register record when a copy states a window. The formal rulespec export is the anchored rows (`anchor_kind <> 'none'`), since rulespec's CommentPeriod needs a proceeding or docket anchor; no export exists yet. A Regulations.gov document is a notice's copy only when its `fr_doc_num` says so, so a copy that omits it stands as its own notice: on the 2026-09-28 inputs about 2,950 such documents share a docket, close day and opening (within three days) with a Register notice. An extension stays its own period when it names its notice by neither page nor RIN, when its title says "extension of time for comments" (the title matcher misses that phrasing), or when its page or RINs name more than one open notice: one extension of two proposals (2022-13209 extends 2022-08993 and 2022-08994 under RINs 0910-AI28 and 0910-AI60) links to neither. A legacy Regulations.gov document whose posting date is decades early (see `documents`) opens its period that early.

current-committee-assignments.coverageStatement: Sampled. Today's seats: the House Clerk's and the Senate's committee files are captured whole each run, for the current Congress only, and each capture replaces its chamber's rows for that Congress; an earlier Congress keeps its last capture. Vacant and placeholder seats appear as the Clerk's file states them.
current-committee-assignments.qualityNotes: A row is a seat the file listed on its `file_date`: a seat the file no longer lists is gone on the next capture. The House file states its Congress and the reader proves it; the Senate file states none, so its rows carry the caller's Congress with `congress_basis` = `caller`. A House vacancy has no member and no row, and a seated member whose only assignment is the file's `<committee rank=""/>` placeholder has none either (nine placeholders on 2026-09-19). Only a file captured this run replaces its chamber's rows; a chamber whose file was not established keeps its prior rows. House `system_code` derives its prefix from the native committee type and parent context. For full joint committees in the 119th Congress, the verified Clerk codes, names and joint type map `JL00` to `jslc00`, `JP00` to `jspr00` and `IT00` to `jstx00`. Other joint codes keep their legacy spelling. `committee_code` preserves the literal source identifier. Join matching `system_code` values to `committees` and `bioguide_id` to `members`. Rows whose `system_code` matches no committee stay listed. Names alone do not establish a join. `EC00` remains unresolved because the Joint Economic Committee has three Congress.gov codes. The 2026-09-23 comparison predates the verified mappings. Its 28 unmatched rows included 25 House seats on `EC00`, `IT00`, `JL00` and `JP00`, and three Senate seats on `JSIK00`, the 2024 inaugural committee for which the comparison found no Congress.gov code.

current-committee-meetings.coverageStatement: Sampled, and accumulating. Congress.gov meeting lists cover the current Congress and updates to the previous Congress. New meeting details are read newest first, at most 1,000 a run. Unread or refused details leave list-only records. The previous Congress remains in scope because published transcripts can update its meetings.
current-committee-meetings.qualityNotes:
A row whose `detail_read` is `false` is list-only: its detail has not been read yet, and every detail-only column is NULL with it. A read detail's list is `[]` where the detail states an empty one and NULL where it states none. Rows read before spicy-docs 0.54.0 spelled both `[]`; each such row is read once more, after a run's own reads and under its cap of 1,000, and until then its `[]` can mean either. Event ids are keyed with their chamber because their uniqueness across chambers is unmeasured (spicy-docs' contract note); the 119th's House and Senate event ids come from different ranges, so an id alone does not say which chamber. The publisher's witness entries can repeat within one meeting, so count people by name, not entries.
**Related bills.** Congress.gov often leaves the related bills off a markup's detail, so `bill_ids_json` names none; the meeting's documents usually still name them, in a `meeting_documents_json` entry whose `documentType` is `Bills and Resolutions`. A bill named only in a meeting document is not in `bill_ids_json`.
**A meeting can carry no committee**: `committee_system_code` and `committees_json` are NULL where the detail names none (Senate Finance's nominations meeting of 2026-07-23, event 338678), so a filter on the committee misses it; search `title` as well. **`meeting_status` is Congress.gov's and can lag**: a hearing the committee rescheduled can stay `Scheduled` under its first date (Senate Finance's trade-agenda hearing, event 338326 on 2026-04-23, which the committee lists as rescheduled to July, event 338681).
**Senate and NoChamber meetings list no witnesses here.** Congress.gov's committee-meeting detail, the route this table reads, has no `witnesses` element for those chambers (retained detail `119/nochamber/338692`), so their witness lists are `[]` or NULL: the route stated none, not that the meeting had none. For a printed hearing, `hearing_transcripts.witnesses_json` lists the witnesses GovInfo's MODS names (CHRG-119shrg64653 names four). A transcript reaches its meeting by `event_id`, or by `mods_event_id` where `event_id` is NULL, with `congress` and `chamber`; most Senate transcripts name no meeting either way, so most Senate meetings have no witness list from either source.
The publisher's `NoChamber` value is stored as `nochamber`, matching its detail address and preserving the existing row identity. It is neither NULL nor an inferred `joint` chamber. The source reader accepts that address, so previously list-only rows can fill at an unchanged timestamp. Retained meeting `119/nochamber/338692` names the Helsinki Commission; the September 24 committee-meetings audit retains its list row and served detail.

current-committee-reports.coverageStatement: Sampled. Selected committee report packages from GovInfo, a mixed-Congress selection that grows as packages are added; not complete historical or constituent-granule coverage. committee_report_reads records each package read and its outcome.
current-committee-reports.qualityNotes: Only the MODS PRIMARY bill fills bill_id. The CBO columns come from spicy-docs read_cbo_estimate on the same body already acquired. The cover recital gates publication of a letter: a CBO heading alone is not an estimate. report_states_estimate=false records an absent recital; NULL means the rule has not run. cbo_letter_count counts the letters located in the part, each a committee_report_cbo_letters row; a positive recital with a count of 0 is a declared estimate no letter was located for, distinct from an extracted letter. The five per-letter columns this table carried until committee_reports legislative-documents/2 (the first letter's span, digest, end rule and signatory) are on committee_report_cbo_letters, one row per letter (ss-uep5). estimate_heading stays here with a two-sided meaning: the part's first estimate heading where no located letter opens on it, NULL where one does (that letter's row carries it). It keeps all 115 headings of live generation 670476640e83 that open no letter, among them 110 undeclared reports' "Congressional Budget Office Cost Estimate" sections saying none was received; the other 29 live headings opened a letter and are on its row. recital_bill_id comes from the printed recital and is retained beside the MODS bill_id. bill_id is the part's own PRIMARY bill: a multi-part package's root states none, so each part of CRPT-119hrpt494 carries the H.R. 3495 its constituent record names, where its row read before parts were keyed has NULL; its separate recital_bill_id is a text interpretation. Every part a record states is read, all or none: a package whose parts cannot all be read is refused in committee_report_reads and keeps its prior rows. Parts, by decision 29 (`docs/research/fork-delivery-decisions-2026-09-22.md`): a report published in one part is one row whose part_id is its package id and whose part_number is NULL; a report published as parts is one row per part, part_id the part's granule id (CRPT-119hrpt455-pt2) and part_number 1 to N, except that a Part 1 the publisher left unsuffixed (CRPT-119hrpt494) has part_id equal to the package id and part_number 1. A package whose one part is spelled -pt1 (CRPT-119hrpt811; spicy-docs `docs/tables.md` names the others it measured) is (package-pt1, 1), the same shape as Part 1 of two, so a reader counts a package's rows to tell a lone part from Part 1 of several. title, date_issued and last_modified are the package's and repeat on every part row. A row published before part_id existed is kept as its package's one part (part_id the package id, part_number NULL) until the package is read again, which replaces its rows as a set; the committee_report_reads rule version re-reads every report once for this, which is what re-keys the CRPT-119hrpt811 row published 2026-09-24 as (CRPT-119hrpt811-pt1, 1).

current-congress-bills.qualityNotes: **Historical cosponsor-count defect:** the 2026-09-21 native-XML audit found 13,154 wrong zero counts in the then-retained 118th Congress HR/S output using SpicyDocs 0.24.2. The current reader counts the publisher's separate cosponsors list, including withdrawn entries, as the column description states. Corrected code does not establish that every historical row has been re-read; consult the selected generation's audit before claiming population-wide repair. Historical receipt: `legislative-release-candidate-2026-09-21/`. `statutes_at_large_cite` is filled at this table's merge by joining the published `laws` table on `bill_id`, as its column sentence says: `bill-family` reads `laws` best-effort after its merge and takes the law's citation where one is published, keeping a citation already here where `laws` has none for the bill; with no `laws` table published the column stays as it was, NULL on a cold start. It is never guessed: `laws` publishes a citation only from a captured PLAW USLM file, and reads a NULL through its own `uslm_outcome`. `public_law_number` and `law_type` are not that case: they come from the bill's own publisher record — its `laws` entry, when the publisher states one — and are filled wherever the bill family has reached. `url_source` `congress_api_list` marks a row the retired list writer last wrote. Its run of 2026-09-23 replaced 3,044 BILLSTATUS `update_date` instants with the list route's same-day dates and 3,095 congress.gov page URLs with API resource URLs (receipt `drift-audit-2026-09-23/`). current-document-citations.coverageStatement: Derived, and selective. Citation occurrences from held House activity reports and budget volumes, plus operator-selected fields from bills, reports, lobbying records, comments, communications and court opinions, at most 100 selected fields per run. `document_citation_read_outcomes` records exact read scopes and successful zero findings. No citation rows can mean unread, refused or no matches; this table is not an inventory of held text. Page-read evidence belongs to receipts, not the main report or budget columns.
current-document-citations.qualityNotes:
**The span is in the identity because the span is the yield.** Keying on document, kind and target alone would collapse CRPT-118hrpt968's repeated mentions of one bill into one row; the aggregate is derivable from this table with `GROUP BY document_key, cite_kind, target_key` and the reverse is not. **A publisher's revisions keep their histories; a new reading of the same bytes does not.** A print whose source bytes changed adds findings beside the earlier text version. A new `text_sha256` from unchanged bytes (a corrected text derivation) replaces the earlier reading, so the same span does not repeat when the checkpoint records the same source SHA. A checkpoint without that hash keeps earlier readings, even under an equal publisher timestamp. Historical duplicates need exact source evidence before reconciliation. A successful rule correction for the same document and text digest replaces that digest's findings, including an empty result; it can retire obsolete rows. A failed read preserves previous findings. Size grows with revisions and their citations. Filter to the digest the document row states (`house_activity_reports.text_sha256` or `budget_volumes.text_sha256`) to read exactly one text. Prints are revised rarely. `stated_by_index` is three-valued and the third value matters: `true`/`false` where a keyed index record was read and could state a key of this shape, and **NULL where no comparison was possible** — either no index record was supplied or the MODS vocabulary has no element of that shape, which is the case for every bill citation of a budget volume. So the consumer predicate for "what the print adds" is `WHERE stated_by_index IS NOT TRUE`, never `= false`. `target_resolved` false means the cite was found and its key is unsettled, not that the cite is wrong. `target_rule` says **how** a key was reached and separates lookups from inferences: `exact` and `roster_prefix` are lookups against a supplied vocabulary, while `name_prefix` and `sibling_prefix` are inferences from the printed text that a consumer may decline. `evidence_page` is NULL where the rendition states no page boundary, and a match straddling a page break is attributed to the page it began on.
**A document with no rows here is not shown to be unheld.** Each held-field kind has rows only for the documents selected so far (on 2026-10-03 the report_section rows covered one of the report packages `report_sections` holds); count distinct `document_key` by `document_kind` for the live figure. GAO product ids join `gao_reports` on `report_number = target_key`, GAO's own spelling (`report_id` is the same id in lower case); the few that do not resolve are `…SU` products, which `gao_reports` does not hold, and misprints such as `GAO-21-105520` (GAO-23-105520 is held).

Calendar searches must distinguish source dates from instants. Under the
Regulations.gov convention in SpicyDocs' `regulations_gov_day`, date-only
values and bare `T00:00:00Z` retain their printed day; other offset-bearing
timestamps use `America/New_York`, not their UTC date. For example,
`2026-10-05T03:59:59Z` is October 4 at 23:59:59 EDT, while
`2026-11-24T04:59:59Z` is November 23 at 23:59:59 EST. This bare-midnight
exception is source-specific, not a rule for arbitrary timestamps.

This guarded DuckDB example selects October 2–16 inclusive in Eastern
calendar days (not a 14-day instant interval). It handles the shown ISO
forms, preserving the source's date-only convention; year zero, malformed
values and offset-free timestamps yield NULL. Inspect those unknowns
separately rather than treating exclusion from the filter as no deadline.
Do not compare UTC timestamp strings with a date-only upper bound.

```sql
WITH calendar AS (
  SELECT document_id,
    CASE
      WHEN left(v, 4) = '0000' THEN NULL
      WHEN regexp_full_match(v, '[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}(T00:00:00Z)?')
        THEN TRY_CAST(left(v, 10) AS DATE)
      WHEN regexp_full_match(v, '[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}T.+(Z|[+-][0-9]{2}:[0-9]{2})')
        THEN CAST(TRY_CAST(v AS TIMESTAMPTZ) AT TIME ZONE 'America/New_York' AS DATE)
    END AS end_day
  FROM (SELECT document_id, trim(comment_end_date) AS v FROM documents)
)
SELECT document_id, end_day FROM calendar
WHERE end_day >= DATE '2026-10-02' AND end_day < DATE '2026-10-17';
```

A date field alone does not establish submission purpose or the legally
controlling/current deadline. For example, FR 2026-15634's DATES text
specifies October 2, 2026 objections/hearing requests under 40 CFR part 178,
not ordinary comments. NULL does not establish that no deadline exists.
Read the notice's filing instructions and later notices before acting.
`fr_docket_links` offers source docket navigation; `comment_periods` offers
derived date-window candidates, not a complete legal extension history.

Rows are additive. The Mirrulations mirror keeps every capture and never
sees a deletion, so a posting Regulations.gov later removes, or moves to
another docket, stays here: on 2026-10-03 FNA-2026-0301-0004, the Utah
notice (FR 2026-18893) filed to the Idaho docket, answered 404 while this
table held it with `withdrawn = 'false'`; Regulations.gov had re-posted it
as FNA-2026-0313-0006, and its four comments appear under both. A daily
step lists every docket with a document posted or modified in the past
week and reads by id each held document the listing omits:
`publisher_status` is `removed` where Regulations.gov answers 404 or 410.
Older dockets are not checked, so NULL means never checked, not still
published. Removed rows stay here; `agency_stats`, `feed_summary`,
`agency_monthly_volume` and `discovery_signals` leave them and their
comments out. Filter `publisher_status IS DISTINCT FROM 'removed'` to do
the same.

current-gao-decisions.qualityNotes:
`released_date` is when GAO released the decision, not when it decided it; `decided_date` is that day, from the Date line of the decision page's caption, so a count by one differs from a count by the other: over the 6,361 pages captured on 2026-10-03 whose caption read, the release came a median 7 days after the decision (1,294 the same day, 219 more than 90 days after; appropriations decisions a median 0), and 24 pages state a release before the decision, as GAO published them. `decided_date` is NULL, and `b_numbers` and `b_numbers_truncated` are the listing's, where no page was read: on 2026-10-03, 2 pages could not be captured, 247 print no caption (a letter, a report, a decision posted without its text) and 6 refuse for a number GAO mistyped on the page or in the listing; that run's journal names each refused page with its reason. `b_numbers_truncated` `true` is a list still cut, as B-412940's 22 listed numbers are (its page carries no decision text). Apply `html.unescape` when matching a `title`. `outcome` is NULL where GAO's listing states no status sentence for a decision, and where it states one spicy-docs' table leaves unmapped (a cost recommendation, an advisory or appropriations opinion and the like); each run's journal counts both.
GAO's own bid protest statistics, in its annual reports to Congress, are not a count of these rows: GAO counts docket numbers (B-numbers) as cases, not decision pages or procurements, per fiscal year, and takes its sustain rate over merit decisions (sustained plus denied). Here a row is one decision page, which can carry several B-numbers, dated by its release. The annual reports are rows of `gao_reports` (`GAO Bid Protest Annual Report to Congress for Fiscal Year …`) with title, date, link and at most a short abstract: their figures are not held. `decision_type` is GAO's label as its listing states it, not a check: GAO also labels a few reports `Bid Protest Decision` (B-423717, its response to section 885 of the FY2025 NDAA, and B-401197, a report to Congress on defense bid protests).

current-house-activity-reports.coverageStatement: Sampled. House committee activity reports: CRPT packages from the 2023-01-01 issue floor whose titles name activity under the shared title rule. Not an earlier-archive census.
current-house-activity-reports.qualityNotes: **The MODS is authoritative for bills, laws and Code sections, and this table's own columns say so.** Read at full page depth across the eight reports spicy-docs sampled, the print named 0 of 1,406 bills, 0 of 174 public laws, 0 of 37 U.S. Code sections and 0 of 7 Statutes at Large pages that the package MODS does not already state — so `distinct_bills_beyond_index`, `distinct_laws_beyond_index` and `distinct_usc_sections_beyond_index` are near zero, and a nonzero one is worth reading the evidence span for rather than taking as new yield. Measured here 2026-09-20 over **41** reports rather than eight, "zero" is very nearly right and not exactly right: 7 print-only bills of 7,686 distinct, 5 print-only laws of 990, and 6 print-only Code sections. The one apparent survivor, `188-11`, was the print's own misprint of `118-11`. What the print does add is committees beyond the submitting one (27 resolved codes), 87 RINs, 38 agency dockets and 5 GAO product ids. **Except for the Congress of a Senate report's bills.** A Senate committee files its report early in the following Congress, and GovInfo stamps the MODS's bills with that filing Congress; printed bills are keyed in `covered_congress`, the Congress the report itself states, so on a Senate report `bills_congress_mismatch` and `distinct_bills_beyond_index` count the MODS's wrong Congress, not new yield (2026-09-26 drift audit: the eight Senate reports on the 117th had published 1,915 citations under 118th-Congress bills before the fix). **And for a House report's bills printed under a Congress subheading.** CRPT-117hrpt705 and -118hrpt974 print a predecessor bill's history under `116th Congress` or `117th Congress` inside the current bill's entry, and -118hrpt967 heads each Congress of its committee history, 107th to 118th, the same way; since spicy-docs `bill_number` 004 those bills are keyed in the subheading's Congress until the next entry, while the MODS stamps them with the filing one, so `bills_congress_mismatch` and `distinct_bills_beyond_index` count them (45 on -117hrpt705, 225 on -118hrpt967; replay receipt `print-subheading-2026-09-26/`). Since `bill_number` 005 a bill the print sets its own Congress beside (`H.R. 6752, 115th Cong.`, `S. Res. 116, 112th Congress`) takes that one ahead of any subheading, and those count the same way (38 citations over the 40 reports; receipt `print-inline-congress-2026-09-26/`). A committee name both chambers hold (`Committee on the Judiciary`, `on the Budget`, `on Veterans' Affairs`, `on Armed Services`, `on Appropriations`) resolves to the chamber of the report's own committee, read off the package id; before 2026-09-26 the House won every such name, and the Senate reports published 1,746 House codes for their own committees, 1,718 of them `hsju00`. A chamber the print names before a committee (`Senate Committee on Armed Services`) selects that chamber's committees instead (76 rows moved, 24 of them `hshm00` to `ssga00`). **Limit:** 7 bare committee names in Senate reports reach a name only the House roster holds and keep the House's code, because the print names no chamber: 5 `hshm00` (a wrapped `Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs`, or its `Committee on Home-` fragment) and 2 `hsso00` (`Select Committee on Ethics`). Read them as ambiguous, not as House committees. Receipt: `fix-print-citations-2026-09-26/replay-qualified.json`. `committees_unresolved` is **a floor, not a defect count**: the Senate `cvc` roster states only the committees its listed senators sit on, so a name it does not reach stays unresolved rather than being guessed. `stated_page_count` is the publisher's own `pages` field and is never re-derived from the bytes; `pages_read` is what the extraction saw, and the two are reported separately on purpose (CRPT-118hrpt965 states 282 and a 60-page read saw 60). `submitted_by_bioguide_id` is NULL where the publisher states the member without an id, which CRPT-118hrpt965 does.

current-house-communications.qualityNotes: A row whose `detail_read` is `false` is list-only: its detail has not been read yet (not reached under the cap, or refused), and every detail-only column is NULL with it, including the scalar and occurrence RIN columns, because the rule was not run. A read detail's list is `[]` where the detail states an empty one and NULL where it states none. Rows read before spicy-docs 0.54.0 spelled both `[]`; each such row is read once more (817 on 2026-10-03, one run). The RIN is an interpretation: `rin_rule` names the rule that fired (`report_nature_rin_label/2`) or `unmatched`, and `rin_matched_text` is the exact text, so a false positive is readable from the row. Every run derives the four RIN columns of each read row again from its retained `report_nature`, re-read or not, so no row keeps an earlier SpicyDocs' scalar or rule name. The rows the `rin_rule` column note says name `report_nature_rin_label` last only until this table's first run under SpicyDocs 0.50.1: after it, no row names the old rule. The publisher repeats a record across a page boundary; the table holds each identity once. The shared pooled list reader must settle each query by distinct identity before any output is replaced. Every existing publisher row receives source_route=congress-gov-detail. Bounded reads of selected Congressional Record issues can fill record_package_id, record_granule_id and record_entry_text from exactly one printed entry with matching Congress, communication type and number. Missing, repeated or incompletely read entries leave these fields empty. The source receipts distinguish unread, failed, empty and ambiguous results. API observations and source_route remain unchanged. Submitting-official and submitting-agency values are not inferred from the printed text.

current-law-code-sections.coverageStatement: Sampled. Every row of each public-law-order table the OLRC classification index links for a scoped Congress, read whole every run and replacing that session's rows. The index links the current Congress's session tables only.
current-law-code-sections.qualityNotes: A row is its position on the page (`seq`), because one line can repeat; a page read this run replaces every prior row for its Congress and session, so a line the publisher removed does not linger under a position it no longer holds. A session not read keeps its rows, and `observed_at` says when they were read. On 2026-10-02 and -03 OLRC answered its classification pages with a maintenance page and status 200, which the reader refuses rather than reading as an empty table. A refused page, or a 401/403, is journaled as `classification-refused` with its URL, status and time, and the nightly `scripts/check_source_refusals.py` fails while the current laws generation holds one; a 401/403 that leaves no session table read also fails the laws run after it publishes. A transport failure is only retried on the next run. Only the public-law order is read: the code-order twin holds the same lines under positions that would collide with these. A Congress the index does not link — every Congress but the current one — gets no rows here; `table3_records` is the historical view. `action` is the page's column 3 verbatim, NULL where the page left it blank, which its legend reads as amended. `usc_section_key` is `usc_section` folded for joins (trimmed, lower-cased, every dash spelling an ASCII hyphen), because case carries no identity in the Code and a join on the printed letter misses the upper-case spellings (decision 30, `docs/research/fork-delivery-decisions-2026-09-22.md`). Every laws run derives `usc_section_key` and `usc_place` again on every row from its stored `usc_section` and `action`, so a session not read keeps current ones; a row meets its `table3_records` record on `law_number` (its `act_key`), title, key and place. A law can be classified in the session table after the one its number suggests (119-70 is in the session-2 table, whose caption names it); filter by `law_id`, not by `session`, and `stated_laws` carries each table's caption.

current-laws.coverageStatement: Sampled. Every law the Congress.gov law route lists for the scoped Congresses (the current one by default), walked whole each run; the PLAW USLM citation is added per law, newest first, under a per-run cap. A steady-state run is meant to ask only about laws whose list row moved or whose PLAW the bulk folder had not yet served.
current-laws.qualityNotes:
`statutes_at_large_cite` is set when `uslm_outcome` is `captured`; read every NULL through `uslm_outcome` and `uslm_reason`. `unavailable` (reason `source_unavailable`) is the publisher's own lag, a `404` from the exact PLAW locator: on 2026-09-19 the route listed 108 laws and the PLAW bulk folder held 104, the four newest (119-103, 119-104, 119-109, 119-110) absent; each is retried every run until the folder serves it.
`captured_partial` is a validated USLM file that states no Statutes at Large citation (reason `statutes_citation_not_stated`): the two private laws of the 119th (`PLAW-119pvtl1`, `PLAW-119pvtl2`), whose own `citableAs` values are kept in `uslm_citable_as`. Until reader rule `laws-uslm-v2` (2026-09-25) the contract refused those two files and their rows said `not_requested`, although both were requested and served. `captured_refused` keeps the digest of a `200` body the reader refused, either another law's file (`native_identity_refused`) or not native USLM at all, such as an HTML page (`native_shape_refused`), and none of its unvalidated fields. `request_failed` is an attempted read that established nothing, a transport failure included; it is never published as `unavailable`. `not_requested` means only that no request was made, which the per-run cap decides.
A validated row with parsed text is read again when its listing or metadata/text reader changes, or its matching section output is missing. A failed later attempt preserves its prior metadata and parsed sections. `law_text_outcome` distinguishes unread, parsed and refused text; an unavailable XML file does not mean the law has no provisions. Join `law_sections` on `law_id` for native sections. `law_body_remainder` retains main-body text outside those sections, including appropriation blocks; it is NULL unless parsed and may be an empty string on success. The section rows and remainder are printed law text, not consolidated current law. A publisher-refused Table III read is journaled `table3-bulk-refused` with reason `access-refused`, and the laws family publishes without the Table III rows that read would have added. `statutes_at_large_volume` follows the session that cleared the bill, not the year the law was approved: 119-69 and 119-71 to 119-73, approved in January 2026 on bills cleared in December 2025, are in volume 139, and 119-70 and 119-74 on are in volume 140. `statutes_at_large_last_page` comes with reader `laws-uslm-v3` (2026-10-03), so a row read under an earlier reader holds NULL there, which means not read, until the next laws run reads its PLAW again. `resolve_document_citations` resolves a Statutes citation to a page inside a law's range to that law and says the match is by range (`match_basis`); a law with no last page is matched by its first page only.

current-member-votes.coverageStatement: Sampled, and accumulating. One row per member per roll call in `roll_call_votes`, so it inherits that table's both-chambers scope, per-run cap and skip-what-is-already-held behavior exactly.
current-member-votes.qualityNotes:
House rows with `state` `XX` are the non-voting delegates and the Resident Commissioner, as the Clerk marks them. The Clerk marks them only on amendment votes and motions in committee, so leave them out when ranking voting Representatives. A member who died before a term began can appear as Not Voting on its opening quorum call, as the Clerk's file lists them. One `bioguide_id` can carry more than one spelling of `member_name`; group by `bioguide_id`. The Clerk's files of 1990-2002 (the 101st-107th Congresses) name no member by bioguide id: their rows key `name:` plus the Clerk's label (`name:Jones (NC)`), and that key identifies the row within its roll call, not a person, since at least 21 labels of those years name two different members. The `bioguide_id` on such a row is resolved at the votes merge, not stated by the Clerk (rule `house-name-crosswalk-v4`): it is the one member of that surname, state and party seated in the House in that Congress, per `members`, `member_terms` and `member_party_affiliations`, and only where the vote's day lies inside that member's term. A printed first name chooses among several members when it equals the crosswalk's, in full, in its first word or as an initial, or when it is the nickname the crosswalk's source states for the member (`Tom` for Thomas Davis), which is read once `members` publishes it. Where several still answer to the label, as a successor of the same surname does (the 105th's Capps and Bono, the 107th's Shuster), the row takes the one of them seated on the vote's day; and on a day that seats several, a label that prints no first name is the member left once those the same roll call lists under a first name are set aside (the 101st's `Smith (OR)` beside `Smith, Denny (OR)`). Anything else stays NULL, and `member_vote_terms` leaves that row `unresolved_member`. Applied to the table published 2026-10-04, the rule resolves 3,173,468 of its 3,175,523 such rows with `members` as published, and 3,175,521 with the source's nicknames: the 101st's two Smiths of Oregon and the 107th's `Davis, Tom` (2,053 rows) wait for that column. The two rows then left are one that prints the Speaker `D` (106-house-1-2) and one dated the day after its member died. Run over the rows of 2003 on with the Clerk's own ids hidden and the source's nicknames, the rule filled 6,567,134 of 6,567,152 and differed from the Clerk on two: 109-house-1-239 and -240, which state M000249 (Robert Matsui, who died before that Congress met) on the row of Doris Matsui (M001163), as Voteview records those two votes. Those rows keep the id the Clerk states. Receipt: fork-execution-2026-09-21/votes-person-crosswalk-2026-10-05/. Senate rows carry the bioguide id resolved from their LIS id through `members` at the votes merge; a Senate row still NULL has a LIS id that `members` does not hold, or holds twice (`unresolved_member`).
The Clerk lists the Speaker only on the roll calls the Speaker votes on; on the others the Speaker has no row at all, not a Not Voting row (Johnson, J000299, has no row on 54 of the 314 House roll calls of 2026, measured 2026-10-03), so an absence rate over roll calls does not apply to the Speaker. `party` is the label the publisher printed on that roll call, and a change of label starts on the roll call that first prints it: the Clerk prints Kiley (K000401) `R` through roll 95 (2026-03-18) and `I` from roll 96 (2026-03-19), while `member_party_affiliations` dates the change 2026-03-09. Use `party` for a split as the chamber recorded it, and `member_party_affiliations` for a party as of a date.

current-org-committee-links.qualityNotes: These are heuristic name matches, not source-reported affiliations. `confidence` grades the matching rule alone, not a measured probability: it does not look at whether the committee still files or at the sponsor FEC states. Links to a candidate's committee (FEC committee type `H`, `S` or `P`) or a member's leadership PAC (designation `D`) are left out, because such a committee is never an organization's own (25 of 25 sampled were false, 2026-10-03). `connected_organization_name` and `sponsor_name_match` add FEC's own statement of each committee's sponsor beside the grade: in a seeded sample of 45 `high` links (2026-10-03, judged from FEC's committee records), 15 of 15 that agree, 13 of 15 that differ and 12 of 15 with no stated sponsor were the commenting organization's own committee or filing. Whether a committee has terminated is in `fec_committees`, one join away on `committee_id`: `filing_frequency` `T` (terminated) or `A` (administratively terminated), and `last_file_date`. A link to a terminated committee can still be right, for a comment filed while the committee was active.

current-press-releases.coverageStatement: Window. Releases from the House and Senate Appropriations committees' feeds as captured since September 19, 2026, including items that later rotated out of a feed; bill links are inferred from release text. Not all committees, earlier history or release-page bodies. See `press-release-qualification/` and `press-link-repair/` in the fork execution receipts.
current-press-releases.qualityNotes: The bill linkage is a pattern match over the release's own words, not a publisher statement. An earlier local run falsely matched `s 2027` inside a reference to the President's 2027 budget to Senate bill 2027. The corrected matcher rejects possessive suffixes while preserving quoted bill citations; wider matching quality remains unmeasured. `matched_field` and `matched_text` carry what was matched and where: a false positive is readable from the row rather than only by re-running the matcher. One pattern is compiled per published bill in the Congresses in scope, bounded on both sides and built from the bill's own type, so a bare number matches nothing. Three states are distinct and must not be read as one: a `bill_id` with `match_rule = bill_number_in_title` or `bill_number_in_excerpt` is a match; `match_rule = unmatched` with a NULL `bill_id` means the matcher ran and found no pattern match; an all-NULL `match_rule` means no matching pass ran at all, because no `congress_bills` table was published when the rollup ran, or none was published for that release's Congress, or the release states no readable `pub_date` to scope by. The Senate feed carries no item description, so a Senate release can only ever match on its title. One consequence worth knowing before relying on these four columns: a run that cannot read `congress_bills` republishes the whole live window with NULL match columns, because this table merges row-wise and a fresh row wins whole. The next run that can read it re-derives them for every release still in the feed, so the gap normally lasts one cycle — but a release that rotates off the feed during that cycle keeps the NULL permanently. The other publisher columns are unaffected; only these four degrade.

current-roll-call-votes.coverageStatement: Sampled, and accumulating. Independent Senate LIS session lists and House Clerk roll files supply votes under per-run caps. The scheduled scope is the current Congress; older Congresses require backfill. Clerk history begins in 1990, in the 101st Congress; bill-derived vote references begin in the 108th. A failed chamber listing preserves its prior rows, so chambers can lag separately. Recent votes may be reread for corrections. Bill references alone do not prove a complete session index. `vote_date` retains publisher spelling and is not a sortable date bound.
current-roll-call-votes.qualityNotes: Two statements link a roll call to a bill, and `match_rule` names the one that did. `bill_action_recorded_vote`: a `recordedVotes` entry on the bill's own action, read from `bill_vote_references`. `vote_file_legislation`: the vote file's own statement of its measure, the Clerk's `legis_num` or the Senate's document, with the file's own URL as `match_url`; on a Senate amendment vote that document is `S.Amdt.`, not a bill, so such a roll call links to a bill only where the rollup resolved one through the bill's own recorded-vote action (`count(bill_id)` over amendment votes is the measure). The bill's action wins; where two bills' actions record one roll call, the one the file names wins (the Senate passing a House bill after its Senate twin); with no recorded reference the file links alone. A procedural question, a nomination, a treaty or two different bills link nothing. Measured on the 108th and 119th (receipt `votes-backfill-2026-09-26/file-links/`), the files add 881 links and agree with the recorded reference on 1,803 of the 1,809 roll calls both link; the six others are those Senate passages. `conflict_count` is per roll call, not per run: it counts the later references, the file's included, that named a different bill for *this* roll call, and they are kept rather than dropped. Before 2003 only the file's `legis_num` links: it links 6,614 of the 7,327 files of 1990-2002 to 2,842 bills, 26 of which have no `congress_bills` row yet. A held row is relinked from its own columns without a fetch; a House row published before `legis_num` or `clerk_body_element` existed is read again once to gain both, with `vote_desc`. A Senate row published before `vote_question_text`, `vote_title`, `majority_requirement` and `modify_date` existed is read again once in the same way and gains them and any tie-breaker: until then its NULL tie-breaker columns say nothing about whether the vote was tied. The scheduled run reads the sitting Congress's such rows; an earlier Congress's are read when its number is dispatched. Replayed over the retained files of the 108th-118th, that read fills the element on all 14,503 published House rows (3,742 `committee`) and `vote_desc` on 9,191, and changes no other column and no member row; it also publishes the five votes the House vacated before recording a position, which have zero tallies, `member_vote_count` 0 and no `member_votes` rows. The Clerk's 2003 Speaker election (108-1-2), whose candidate totals contradict its members' choices, still refuses. The contract's `house_vote_legislation` rule (Congress.gov's `house-vote` listing) is no longer produced and no published row carries it: it was retired with the api.data.gov key it needed (2026-09-26). Each run fills a NULL `vote_day` on every held (completely captured) roll call from its own `vote_date` before merging, so a row published before the column existed gains it without a re-fetch. An incomplete capture is not held: it is re-fetched first each run and takes its day from the file. A linkage-only row keeps NULL.

current-rulemaking-lifecycles.coverageStatement: Derived, and bounded by its inputs: every docketed proceeding, paired from its cleaned `lifecycle_events` and censored at the day its inputs end.

historicalDeclaredChecks.name: lifecycle-outcomes
historicalDeclaredChecks.population: All-stratum non-NULL outcomes only, plus global NULL-agency cell; separate routine strata are overlapping.
historicalDeclaredChecks.selection_policy: Matching declared input bytes or one materialized/catalog export snapshot; fixed comment URLs require unchanged ETags around the read. Each check selects its own pins.

current-rulemaking-lifecycles.qualityNotes:
A Regulations.gov document that states no Register number in `fr_doc_num`, or whose stated number resolves to no Register row, is dated by its upload, which for a legacy document can be years after the rule: on snapshot_9b2c770e's inputs 262 lifecycles anchor on such a document, 74 of them upload pairs outside survival (docs/ontology.md). A proposal typed only by Regulations.gov (`lifecycle_events.source = 'regulations_gov'`, an unnumbered upload) can be a petition for rulemaking, a state program submission or an information-collection notice the Register files under another type: on snapshot_62318069's inputs 515 survival lifecycles since 2015 anchor on one (352 open); a Register number its title names is not read as its identity. Where the proceeding also holds the Register's proposal, the Register's anchors (54d); an upload keeps its anchor when a final falls between the two or the Register's is a comment-period extension or correction, so an earlier proposal whose Register copy is missing may still anchor on its later re-proposal (FDA's 1978 OTC-monograph dockets re-proposed in the 1990s). A final that finalizes another docket's proposal is paired in its own proceeding only and the proposal stays `open`: a RIN never groups dockets (56a), and the Register's docket labels are often an agency's own (2026-15833 names 'CMS-1849-F and CMS-0062-F' and no RIN). A Register proposal naming several dockets anchors one lifecycle per docket (502 proposals behind 2,358 of 35,327 survival rows on snapshot_62318069's inputs; EPA 20%). A posting Regulations.gov flags withdrawn (`documents.withdrawn`) anchors nothing: it was misfiled, duplicated, moved or replaced, and the Register publishes an agency's withdrawal of a rule as a document of its own.
For `routine_family` `pesticide_tolerance` the proposal is usually EPA's notice that it received a pesticide petition (FFDCA 408(d)(3)), typed Proposed Rule, not a proposal of rule text: 443 of the 459 EPA tolerance lifecycles proposed since 2020 on snapshot_448e6d9a's inputs. Time to final then runs from the receipt notice, and `proposal_form` does not tell the two apart.
FDA's notices that it filed a food or color additive petition ("Filing of Food Additive Petition", "… Color Additive Petition") are the same case with no stratum: the Register types them Proposed Rule (its `action`, "Notification of petition.", is not carried by `federal_register`), `routine_family` is NULL, and on snapshot_55d396ee's inputs 64 of the 199 FDA lifecycles proposed since 2018, and 130 of the 831 in the published FDA cell, anchor on one. Match the proposal's Register title (`filing of … petition`) to set them apart. A count of lifecycles counts docketed proceedings, not rulemakings: FNA's three open lifecycles on that snapshot are one RIN, 0584-AF22, in dockets FNA-2026-0034, -0166 and -0201; count distinct `proceedings.rin` for rulemakings.

current-sam-entities.qualityNotes: A row is a registration, keyed by `uei` and `entity_eft_indicator`: one entity registers once per EFT indicator (187 of the 147,038 UEIs in the 2026 extract carry more than one), so `uei` alone is not unique. A file with fewer registrations than it declares, less those credits, is refused. A year read retires the registrations it no longer holds (80 expired from 2002 and 2003 and 11 from 2026 on 2026-09-26), journaled as `rows-retired` so qualification reconciles every removal. current-section-diffs.coverageStatement: Sampled: consecutive printings of a bill are compared only when both bodies were acquired and parsed, from the Congresses the bill family has read.
current-section-diffs.qualityNotes: A consecutive pair that cannot be diffed — because one or both sides has no parsed tree — is a counted refusal named by table, never a row. Measured on the cold-start run of the 119th (receipt `d1-measured-run-2026-09-19/`): **3,185** refusals against 128 published comparisons, which is what a 600-printing cap over 22,064 printings implies, since a pair needs both of its sides fetched in the same run. A pair runs from a printing to its neighbour in spicy-docs' `printing_order`: publisher date, then a dateless enrolled printing by its stage (`pair_rule` `consecutive_by_date_then_stage`). A pair's neighbour can be a procedural printing (a four-section Senate engrossed amendment between the calendar printing and the enrolled bill), which the summary route refuses but this table compares, so the pair reads as nearly everything removed and then everything added. In `section_diff_items`, `financial_amounts_changed` is true on every added or removed row that carries a figure, by construction; only a modified row says a figure changed in place. Floor-amendment annotations (`(increased by $X)`) are left out of `financial_*_amounts_json` though they change the text; `financial_has_amendment_annotations` marks them. Enrolled printings carry new element ids at the publisher, so `element_id` does not join into `enr`.

current-senate-expenditures.coverageStatement: Sampled. GovInfo CDOC expenditure reports from the 2024-01-01 issue floor, limited by a per-run package cap and the first 80 pages of each file. Counts are lower bounds. Part I and Part II repeat summary pages before diverging into detailed statements. The later compensation and mail-allocation sections lie outside this page window. Page-limit evidence is retained separately from the printed main rows.
current-senate-expenditures.qualityNotes:
**Most rows carry one cell, not a row of cells, and `cells_ruled` is how you tell.** Of the ruled body rows across the pages spicy-docs measured when it wrote the contract (release 0.23.0), those in an `appropriation_summary` grid carry all nine cells and every other one carries exactly **one** cell of ten or of seven: the print rules a whole payee block as a single cell. That is why the contract has no `payee_name`, `document_number`, `date_posted` or singular `amount` column — those would be a parse of one cell's newlines presented as separate facts. `WHERE cells_ruled` selects the rows whose cells are separate facts; everything else is in `cells` exactly as printed. **`cells` is the row**; every other content column is a promotion out of it. `office`, `funding_year`, `appropriation_title` and `section_heading` are read from the page text and are **NULL on a continuation page**, which is 56 of the 139 measured table pages — forward-fill them in `printed_page` order. `printed_page`, not `page`, is what the report's own contents index by. `grid_kind` is NULL where the first row states none of the three known labels, so an unrecognised grid is visible rather than mislabelled. An amount must carry a decimal point to be parsed into `amounts`: without that rule a bare integer read stacked fiscal years and account numbers as money, and every amount-shaped line measured carries a `.dd` tail while the lines that do not are all account numbers or fiscal years. The check that makes the extraction falsifiable is the print's own `Totals` row, which agreed to the cent with the sum of its account rows over seven money columns on both measured sections.
**What each package's read window holds.** Part I's pages reach the `A-` summary and the leadership and officers' `B-` pages; Part II's reach a short alphabetical run of senators' offices (in GPO-CDOC-119sdoc6: Justice, Kaine, Kelly and Kennedy), so a Senate-wide or other senator's figure is not here; `SELECT DISTINCT office` for the package says which offices are. The `A-` summary is by appropriation account only, with no object-class (travel and the like) rollup: object classes are in each office's `ORGANIZATION TOTALS` block. One report period's spending is spread over one block per funding year (FY2024, FY2025 and FY2026 in the October 2025 to March 2026 report), so sum the blocks' period amounts. A zero prints as `$.00`.
A payroll cell can interleave two printed lines letter by letter ("D SEIR NE AC TT OO RR" for DIRECTOR and SENATOR, on GPO-CDOC-119sdoc5-2 page B-1470 and 119sdoc6-2 page B-1262), so the cells hold the print exactly for the amounts, which stayed intact, and not always for the text.

current-table3-records.coverageStatement: Window, complete for the Congresses read: every public law Table III holds for each Congress the laws table holds, plus the scoped ones, derived from OLRC's Table III bulk file on each run, so a Congress keeps its rows current after it leaves the laws scope while Table III catches up. The file holds the whole table back to 1789; other Congresses, private laws and pre-1957 session-law chapters are not derived.
current-table3-records.qualityNotes:
Table III holds an act only once OLRC has classified it, and lags enactment: on 2026-09-26 it was current through 119-73, a law of 2026-01-23, while the law route reached 119-111. `release_point` says how current the file was. Its file at release point 119-73 also has no record of 119-70, a second-session law `law_code_sections` classifies (OLRC's gap, not a reading error).
Since 2026-09-26 the rows come from the bulk file (`fulldump@<release point>.xml`) instead of one page per act. The file splits an act's records about ten to an `<act>` fragment. An act's rows are its fragments' records in the file's order, and `seq` is a record's position in its act, as on the page; the file's own `sequence` attribute repeats within 70 acts, so it is not used. Each fragment states its own Congress, date and Statutes volume, and a record carries its fragment's volume where it states a page. Replayed against the 2,981 rows the pages had published, every row keeps its position, act section, Statutes page and volume, Code title and section, status and release point. The file also holds 119-30 and 119-53, whose pages the page walk never reached. Four act-level columns now carry the file's spelling instead of the page's: `stated_key` `119-37` (page `119–37`), `congress` `119` (`119th Cong.`), `act_date` `2025-11-12` (`Nov. 12, 2025`) and `statutes_at_large_volume` `139` (`139 Stat.`).
OLRC states no Last-Modified, ETag or Content-Length for the zip, so each run fetches it; it was byte-identical on 2026-09-14 and 2026-09-26 at the same release point. Each Congress keeps a checkpoint in the file's metadata: the derivation rule with a digest of SpicyDocs' code (not its release string, so a version-only release derives nothing), the member's digest and release point, and each act's shaped-row digest. While all match, nothing is derived. Otherwise every scoped act is derived again, and only an act whose rows changed is published, its whole row set replaced.
Table III only grows: across the eight consecutive releases from 116-150 (2020-07) to 119-73, archived by the Wayback Machine, no act was ever dropped (receipt `table3-bulk-2026-09-26/wayback/`). So a held act the file no longer lists loses its rows only when the release point advances, at most one act a release, and the removal is journaled as `rows-retired` for qualification to reconcile. A file whose release point is older than the one published, that drops an act without advancing, or that drops more than one is refused, and so is a file the reader refuses outright: the member has been renamed twice since 2020. A refused read publishes nothing for this table and keeps every checkpoint, while `laws` and `law_code_sections` publish as usual. The build journals it as `table3-bulk-refused`, and the nightly `scripts/check_source_refusals.py` fails while the current laws generation holds one, so the table cannot stop updating in silence. A transport failure is only retried on the next run. `usc_section_key` is the bare section folded for joins (trimmed, lower-cased, every dash spelling an ASCII hyphen), because case carries no identity in the Code and Table III itself prints some sections both ways (decision 30, `docs/research/fork-delivery-decisions-2026-09-22.md`); the note or preceding words Table III prints inside `usc_section` are in `usc_place` (until 2026-10-03 they stayed in the key, on 1,121 of 2,983 rows). Every laws run derives both again on every row from its stored `usc_section`, so held rows need no read of the file for them.
